lesson.title: Artificial Selection: When Humans Do the Choosing
lesson.summary: Artificial selection relies on the same underlying process as natural selection, heritable variation combined with differential reproduction, except that humans, not the environment, decide which individuals get to reproduce.
lesson.body:
Natural selection requires heritable variation and differences in reproductive success driven by the environment. Artificial selection runs on exactly the same underlying logic, heritable variation exists within a population, and individuals with certain traits leave more offspring than others, with one key difference: humans act as the environment. Rather than survival and reproduction in the wild determining which genotypes have the highest relative fitness, a breeder decides directly which individuals get to reproduce, based on whatever traits they want to favor, whether that is coat color in dogs, milk yield in cattle, or seed size in a crop plant.

Darwin himself leaned on artificial selection as both evidence and analogy, as covered in the chapter on his observations. He bred pigeons personally and studied dog and livestock breeding closely, and he used the striking diversity produced by artificial selection, from fantail pigeons to distinct dog breeds, as a demonstration that selection, applied consistently generation after generation, could produce dramatic change starting from a single ancestral population. If human breeders could accomplish that much within a single lifetime, Darwin reasoned, then nature, acting through the same basic process over the vastly longer timescales that Lyell's geology had made plausible, could produce the full diversity of life on Earth.

The examples are easy to see all around us. Every modern dog breed, from a chihuahua to a great dane, descends from a common ancestor in wolves, yet breeds differ enormously in size, shape, behavior, and coat, the result of intense selective breeding by humans for particular traits over thousands of years. Familiar vegetables tell a similar story, cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, and brussels sprouts are all derived from a single wild mustard relative species, selected over many generations for different parts of the plant, leaves in one case, flower buds in another, stems in a third. Corn, or maize, was domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte through generations of selection by early farmers for larger, more numerous kernels, producing a plant that looks strikingly different from its wild ancestor.

The larger lesson is that artificial selection demonstrates, in a timeframe short enough for humans to observe directly, that the same mechanism Darwin proposed for nature genuinely works, heritable variation plus consistent, differential reproduction really can reshape a population dramatically over generations. That is part of why it served Darwin so effectively as evidence, and why it still works today as one of the clearest, most concrete illustrations of how selection of any kind, natural or artificial, actually changes populations over time.
